title: Marching to McAllister Street

place.label: Third Baptist Church, 1399 McAllister Street (at Pierce)

hook: In 1952 the oldest Black Baptist congregation in the West tore down a pioneer's mansion with its own hands, and marched in to a modern church.
story: Third Baptist began in 1852 as the First Colored Baptist Church of San Francisco, the first African American Baptist congregation west of the Rockies [1]. For almost half a century after 1906 it worshipped at 1299 Hyde Street, far from the wartime Black neighborhood growing up in the Western Addition [2]. In 1950 Rev. Frederick D. Haynes Sr. led the purchase of the northwest corner of Pierce and McAllister, where Captain Charles Goodall's 1859 mansion stood [1]. A newspaper photo caption described congregation members demolishing the house themselves and planning to reuse much of its old timber in the new church [1]. William F. Gunnison designed the sanctuary, with a bell tower and bare cross visible from blocks away; the permit was approved in May 1952 and the building finished that year [1]. A 1953 account recalled how members, fresh from their centenary, "sang their last praises in the old church, and marched in a phalanx to the new." Deborah Johnson, the youngest member, cut the ribbon [1]. Only a few years later the city's other pioneer Black churches followed it west [1][2]. The city made the complex Landmark No. 275 in 2017 [3].

title: The Preacher Who Ran for City Hall
hook: Two decades before San Francisco seated a Black supervisor, a Baptist pastor ran three times, and in 1951 he won 36,000 votes.
story: Frederick Douglas Haynes was born in Talcott, West Virginia, in 1899 and orphaned as a child. He took the pulpit of Third Baptist in 1932, when, a 1953 profile said, most members were unemployed and "often the Sunday offering did not exceed thirty dollars" [1]. By his death in 1971 the church had more than 3,000 members [1]. In 1945 Haynes became the first African American to run for the San Francisco Board of Supervisors, and he ran again in 1947 and 1951 [1]. One campaign flyer read: "I have pledged myself to fight to my dying day to wipe out discrimination against minority races in the economical, political, and social life of our city, state, and nation" [1]. He never won, but his 36,000 votes in 1951, backed by the Union Labor Party, the CIO Council and the Fillmore Democratic Club, showed white politicians that Black voters counted [1][3]. The city context statement names him among the ministers who served as the community's main liaisons with the white power structure [2]. Terry Francois became the first Black supervisor in 1964, and in 1972 Haynes's widow, Charlie Mae, won a seat on the school board [1].

title: A Pulpit for Du Bois and Robeson
hook: When other San Francisco venues would not have Paul Robeson, a church at McAllister and Pierce did. W.E.B. Du Bois came too.
story: Under Rev. F.D. Haynes, Third Baptist became a stage for nationally known Black figures, intellectuals and artists [1]. Du Bois and his wife, the author Shirley Graham Du Bois, chose the church for their West Coast lectures and for Du Bois's 90th birthday celebration; a 1958 photograph shows him addressing the congregation [1]. Dr. Carlton Goodlett, publisher of the Sun-Reporter and a trustee of the church, stayed in close touch with Paul and Eslanda Robeson, and was largely responsible for bringing Robeson to Third Baptist for a concert when all other venues were closed to him [2]. Josephine Baker also appeared there, and a 1958 program advertised Mahalia Jackson [1]. That year Haynes and his church hosted the National Baptist Convention, more than 25,000 Baptists [1]. In the spring of 1960 Haynes invited Martin Luther King Jr. and Ralph Abernathy to a citywide mass meeting on the treatment of minority youth in San Francisco's schools [1]. Others who used its pulpit included Adam Clayton Powell and King himself [3].

title: Leola King's Blue Mirror

place.label: 935 Fillmore Street, between Fulton and McAllister (site)

hook: An Oklahoma-born barbecue cook they called Goldie opened a lounge where Louis Armstrong and Dinah Washington played, then spent decades fighting the bulldozers.
story: Leola King was born in Seminole County, Oklahoma, in 1919 and came to San Francisco in 1946 [1][2]. Friends called her Goldie. Her first hit was Oklahoma King's, a barbecue at 1601 Geary that smoked buffalo, deer and quail [1]. In 1953 she opened the Blue Mirror at 935 Fillmore, between Fulton and McAllister, among the first nightclubs in the Bay Area owned by a woman of color [1][3]. It had a circular bar, velvet festoons and molded Greek figurines [1]. Louis Armstrong, Dinah Washington, Lena Horne, Count Basie and Duke Ellington passed through, and pianist Earl Grant played Monday nights [1][3]. Touring performers slept nearby at the Manor Plaza Hotel, 930 Fillmore [4]. Redevelopment took almost everything: Oklahoma King's was taken for about $25,000, the Blue Mirror closed in the early 1960s, and a sheriff evicted her from a later bar in 1974 [1]. "The way they took everything is criminal," she said [1]. For more than half a century she lived in a 29-room house at 711 Scott Street, on Alamo Square [1]. She died in 2015, aged 96 [3].

title: The Booker T., Where the Stars Slept

place.label: Booker T. Washington Hotel, 1540 Ellis Street (site, near Fillmore)

hook: Often unwelcome in downtown hotels, Nat King Cole, Dinah Washington and W.E.B. Du Bois checked into a six-story hotel off Fillmore, where Slim Gaillard sometimes ran the kitchen.
story: The six-story, 115-room building at 1540 Ellis opened in 1910 as a rooming house. In the 1940s, as the Hotel Edison, it had a notorious reputation [1]. In August 1951 it was remodeled at a cost of $100,000 and renamed the Booker T. Washington Hotel [1]. Accounts differ over who owned what: one credits a buyer named William Bush, another says the colorful Shirley "Fats" Corlett renamed it and the promoter Charles Sullivan bought it [1][2]. What is agreed is that its lobby lounge, booked by Sullivan, became a jazz room; saxophonist Ben Webster opened it on January 31, 1952 [1]. At a time when downtown hotels often turned Black guests away, the Booker T. was where they stayed [3]. A 1953 Sun-Reporter list of guests included Louis Jordan, the Nat King Cole Trio, Dinah Washington, Joe Louis, the Harlem Globetrotters and W.E.B. Du Bois, and Slim Gaillard would take over the kitchen to cook for musicians [1]. Sullivan, the self-made "Mayor of Fillmore," was found shot dead south of Market in 1966; police called it suicide, but the coroner disagreed [2]. The hotel was torn down in 1970, and its address no longer exists [1][3].

title: Mirror Balls at the Primalon Ballroom

place.label: Primalon Ballroom, 1223 Fillmore Street (site, between Turk and Eddy)

hook: A 1930s miniature golf course and roller rink on Fillmore became the ballroom where Count Basie, Lionel Hampton and Dizzy Gillespie played to dancing crowds.
story: The big indoor-outdoor lot at 1223 Fillmore Street opened in 1934 as the Woodland Dancing Hall, complete with miniature golf links [1]. After the Second World War it became the Brown Bomber Café, a beer garden with roller skating on weekdays and, on weekends, skating and dancing together under suspended mirror balls [1]. In 1949 it became the Primalon Ballroom, run by the McCoy family [1][2]. Top acts included Count Basie, Lionel Hampton and Dizzy Gillespie, alongside local blues bands such as Pee Wee Crayton's [1]. Like the Majestic up the street, which became the Fillmore Auditorium in 1952, the Primalon was one of the dance halls that shifted its bookings toward jazz, blues and R&B [2]. The Primalon closed in 1961, and the structure was torn down in 1974 [1]. Nothing of it survives today [2].

title: Behind the Counter at Melrose Records

place.label: Melrose Record Shop, 1226 Fillmore Street (site, between Turk and Eddy)

hook: Before she was famous as Maya Angelou, a young woman sold jazz and blues records on Fillmore Street, beside a Louisiana Navy veteran who would open nightclubs.
story: Not every landmark of the Harlem of the West was a nightclub. At the Melrose Record Shop, 1226 Fillmore Street, neighbors bought the latest jazz and blues, and classical records too [1]. A photograph by David Johnson shows the shopfront around 1950 [2]. In the 1950s one of the clerks was a young woman who would become Maya Angelou; in the same years she was dancing professionally at the Purple Onion in North Beach [1]. Later, in I Know Why the Caged Bird Sings, she wrote about the Fillmore's clubs and bars [1]. Working alongside her was Joseph "Bunny" Simon, born in 1928 into a family of 16 in Lake Charles, Louisiana. He had joined the Navy at 15, was badly injured at Port Chicago, and settled in San Francisco after his discharge in 1946 [3]. It was his part-time job at Melrose that made clear his passion was music. He went on to open nightclubs of his own, starting on Divisadero Street in 1961 [3]. Like most of the business district around it, the shop's building was later demolished [1].

title: Jazz Moves West to Divisadero

place.label: Divisadero and McAllister streets (site of The Playpen)

hook: In the 1960s a string of small jazz rooms opened on Divisadero, where Miles Davis, Wes Montgomery and Ike and Tina Turner played.
story: In 1961 Joseph "Bunny" Simon, a former clerk at the Melrose Record Shop, opened his first club at Divisadero and McAllister. It became known as The Playpen [1]. In a neighborhood torn apart by redevelopment, it was a place where everyone in the Fillmore could gather. Neighbors lined up around the block to drink and dance to the jukebox, and teenagers were let in with chaperones on Sunday afternoons [1]. Upstairs, Redd Foxx, Miles Davis, Wes Montgomery, Sly and the Family Stone and Ike and Tina Turner performed [1]. Simon liked to tell how young Willie Brown opened a campaign office across the street in the early 1960s, and blamed losing the election partly on volunteers who spent their days in the club [1]. Others followed. The Both/And opened at 350 Divisadero in 1965, where Dexter Gordon and Archie Shepp made live records, and in 1967 Herman Warren opened the Half Note in a former coffee shop, with Thelonious Monk among its players [2]. The clubs were friendly rivals: each fielded a softball team, and the losers drank at the winners' bar [2].

title: The Sun-Reporter's Upstairs Room on Turk

place.label: 1366 Turk Street (site of Dr. Goodlett's office and the Sun-Reporter)

hook: A doctor who won a newspaper in a poker game moved it to Turk Street, where Malcolm X, Muhammad Ali and future mayors came upstairs.
story: Dr. Carlton B. Goodlett came to San Francisco in 1945 and opened a medical practice. He soon invested with the dentist Daniel Collins in the Reporter, a Black paper founded in the Fillmore during the war [1]. The paper's longtime editor, Thomas Fleming, later told the story of how they got a second paper, the Sun: its white owner lost about $2,500 to Goodlett at poker one night and offered him the Sun for $1,500 [2]. The two papers became the Sun-Reporter, with the motto "That no good cause shall lack a champion, and that evil shall not thrive unopposed" [2]. The sources disagree on some early dates. In 1963 Goodlett moved both his medical office and the paper to his new building at 1366 Turk Street [1][2]. Its upstairs Community Room became a hub: Malcolm X, Muhammad Ali, Dick Gregory and the Black Panthers came through, and politicians from Willie Brown to George Moscone stopped by for advice [2]. Goodlett also led the local NAACP and in 1966 ran for governor, finishing third in the Democratic primary [1][2]. He died in 1997. The Turk Street building is gone [1].

title: A.M.E. Zion Rebuilds on Golden Gate

place.label: First A.M.E. Zion Church, 2159 Golden Gate Avenue

hook: Pushed off Geary by redevelopment, one of the city's three pioneer Black churches rebuilt in modern style near Masonic Avenue in 1960.
story: Before the war, most middle-class Black San Franciscans belonged to one of three pioneer churches: Third Baptist, Bethel A.M.E., or A.M.E. Zion [1]. A.M.E. Zion had long stood on Pacific Avenue near Powell until the 1906 disaster destroyed it. In 1912, led by the influential Rev. W.J. Byers, the congregation moved to a new church at 1669 Geary Street, at Webster, in the Western Addition [1]. Its ministers, among them the Revs. J.J. Byers and E.J. Magruder, served as leading public voices for the community [1]. As redevelopment advanced, the Geary Street church was demolished in the late 1950s [1][2]. In 1960 the congregation rebuilt at 2159 Golden Gate Avenue, in a building designed by architect Robert Batchelor that cost $130,000 [1]. Like Third Baptist on McAllister eight years earlier, it broke with traditional church design, with simple geometric forms, a flat inset facade, a prominent tower, a bare cross and a vertical panel of square colored windows [2]. The building still stands [1].

title: Bethel A.M.E. Leaves Chinatown for Laguna
hook: After most of a century on Powell Street in Chinatown, a pioneer Black congregation followed its people west, then helped house them.
story: Bethel A.M.E. was one of San Francisco's three pioneer African American churches. Since the nineteenth century it had worshipped at 1207 Powell Street in Chinatown [1]. After the war the old downtown churches were full, and far from where the city's fast-growing Black population now lived. One by one their pastors moved to the Western Addition [1]. In the late 1950s Bethel bought an old, disused church building on Laguna Street. When that grew too cramped, the congregation replaced it with a new church, which it moved into in 1969 [1][2]. Like Third Baptist and A.M.E. Zion, the new building rejected traditional church architecture in favor of strong, simple geometric shapes and plain walls [2]. Bethel then became a builder. During the Western Addition A-2 redevelopment it partnered with the Redevelopment Agency on affordable housing [2]. It sponsored Freedom West, the area's largest co-op, spread over four blocks at the church's corner, and also operates Laurel Gardens, Prince Hall Apartments, Thomas Paine Square and Fellowship Manor [3].

title: Panther Breakfasts in the Parish Hall

place.label: Sacred Heart Church, 554 Fillmore Street (at Fell)

hook: In 1969 a Catholic parish at Fillmore and Fell gave its basement kitchen to the Black Panthers, and the FBI planted evidence there.
story: The streets around Sacred Heart had long been mostly Irish, Eastern European and Italian, but the war changed them [1]. A 1943 parish report noted "rooming house conditions" nearby, and by 1945 Black and Chinese families were buying property on Fell and Fillmore [1]. Wartime migrants included many Black Catholics from Louisiana, and Sacred Heart was one of the parishes where they worshipped [2]. The Black Panther Party approached most of the churches in the area about hosting its free breakfast program. According to pastor Eugene Boyle, they "finally came to us on a lark" [1]. On March 10, 1969, the basement hall and kitchen opened to feed 75 to 100 children a day, many of them students at the parish school [1]. Silent film footage from that year shows the breakfasts under way [3]. That year police told a U.S. Senate committee that the Panthers were handing out a coloring book showing police as pigs. The Panthers had printed a few copies but never distributed them. It was later shown that the FBI planted the books in the church basement as part of its campaign against the party [1].

title: Fifteen to a Room: The Wartime Fillmore

place.label: Fillmore Street between McAllister and O'Farrell

hook: In one decade San Francisco's Black population grew about tenfold, as shipyard workers from Texas and Louisiana crowded into the flats along Fillmore Street.
story: In 1940 San Francisco had 4,806 African American residents. By 1950 it had 43,460, an increase of about 900 percent [1]. They came from Texas, Louisiana, Oklahoma and across the South for work at Hunters Point Naval Shipyard and Marinship in Sausalito. Racial covenants and prejudice closed off many neighborhoods to them, so many settled in the Fillmore [1][2]. By 1950 about 15,000 lived in the Western Addition [2]. Conditions were grim. A 1944 survey by the San Francisco Reporter found war workers "crowded 9, 10, and 15 to a single room with only one window" [1]. Sociologist Charles S. Johnson reported that neighborhood groups and merchants were working to "restrict the area of living for Negro families to the present boundaries of the Fillmore district" [1]. Newcomers spread south along Fillmore and Webster toward Hayes Valley [3]. An eight-block stretch of Fillmore, from Sutter down to McAllister, had already become the main street of Black San Francisco [1]. The newcomers' churches, clubs and shops would soon earn the district a new nickname: the Harlem of the West [1].
